sections.title: Putting It Together
sections.content: Age and date sentences join easily with 'y': '*Tengo* *veinticinco* *años* y mi *cumpleaños* es el *doce* de *mayo*.' A birthday also brings talk of travel and tradition — '*cada* *país* *tiene* *tradiciones* *diferentes*' uses the same 'tener' you already know, just with a plural thing that is had.

items.spanish: Tengo veinticinco años y mi cumpleaños es el doce de mayo.
items.english: I'm twenty-five and my birthday is on the twelfth of May.

items.spanish: El próximo mes hacemos un viaje juntos.
items.english: Next month we're taking a trip together.

items.spanish: Hay un mapa en la pared.
items.english: There's a map on the wall.

sections.content: '*Cada* *país* *tiene* *tradiciones* *diferentes*' still uses 'tener' — a country 'has' traditions the same way a person 'has' an age.

sections.title: Joining more sentences: pero, con, sin
sections.content: 'y' joins two things that go together. 'pero' (but) joins two things that contrast. 'con' means 'with' and 'sin' means 'without' — both go directly before a noun, no linking word needed.

items.spanish: Quiero viajar, pero no tengo tiempo.
items.english: I want to travel, but I don't have time.
We're taking the trip with Daniela.

sections.content: 'pero' contrasts two full ideas: 'Quiero viajar, pero no tengo tiempo.' 'con' and 'sin' just attach to one noun: 'con Daniela', 'sin mapa' — no extra word needed, unlike English 'with/without a...'.
